title: Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics
description: Classical thermodynamics, from the laws and potentials to phase equilibria, solutions and equilibrium, and statistical mechanics, which explains it all from the properties of molecules.

entries.name: The laws of thermodynamics and heat engines
entries.tagline: Four laws that set the limits on energy, heat and work.

facts: If A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is with C. This defines temperature.
Energy is conserved: ΔU = q + w. Internal energy is a state function.

The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Clausius: heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot. Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic process can turn heat from a single reservoir completely into work.
The entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at 0 K, so absolute entropies exist. Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.

sections.text: An engine takes heat q_h from a hot reservoir at T_h, does work w, and gives up heat q_c to a cold reservoir at T_c. The efficiency is η = w ÷ q_h. The Carnot cycle (two isothermal and two adiabatic steps, all reversible) is the most efficient engine that can work between two temperatures.

An engine working between 500 K and 300 K has a maximum efficiency of 1 − 300/500 = 40%. No real engine can exceed this, and real engines are lower, because of irreversibility. Raising T_h or lowering T_c improves it.
A refrigerator is an engine running backward, using work to move heat from cold to hot. Its coefficient of performance, at best, is T_c ÷ (T_h − T_c).

quiz.q: What is the maximum efficiency of an engine operating between 600 K and 300 K?

entries.name: Thermodynamic potentials
entries.tagline: U, H, A and G: four energy functions, each suited to a different set of conditions.

facts: dU = T dS − p dV. Natural variables S and V.
dH = T dS + V dp. Natural variables S and p.
dA = −S dT − p dV. Natural variables T and V.
dG = −S dT + V dp. Natural variables T and p.

points: At constant temperature and volume: dA ≤ 0.
At constant temperature and pressure: dG ≤ 0, so G is the most useful in chemistry, where reactions are run in open vessels.
Equilibrium is the minimum of the appropriate potential.

sections.text: −ΔA is the maximum work that a process at constant T can do, and −ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work (for example electrical work) at constant T and p. That is why G is called the free energy.
If a potential is known as a function of its natural variables, all the other thermodynamic properties follow by differentiation. For G(T, p), S = −(∂G/∂T)_p and V = (∂G/∂p)_T.

quiz.q: Which potential is minimized at equilibrium at constant T and p?

entries.name: Maxwell relations and thermodynamic identities
entries.tagline: Relationships between derivatives that let you calculate hard-to-measure quantities from easy ones.

sections.text: Because U, H, A and G are state functions, their differentials are exact, so the mixed second derivatives are equal. This gives the Maxwell relations:

points: Thermodynamic equation of state: (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂p/∂T)_V − p. For an ideal gas this is zero, so the internal energy of an ideal gas does not depend on volume. For a van der Waals gas it is a n²/V².
Heat capacities: C_p − C_V = TVα²/κ_T, where α is the thermal expansion coefficient and κ_T the isothermal compressibility. For an ideal gas it is nR.
Gibbs–Helmholtz equation: [∂(G/T)/∂T]_p = −H/T². It gives how ΔG and so equilibrium constants depend on temperature.

sections.text: When a gas expands through a throttle (a porous plug) with no heat exchange, the enthalpy stays constant. The temperature change per pressure drop is the Joule–Thomson coefficient μ_JT = (∂T/∂p)_H. An ideal gas does not change in temperature. A real gas cools if it is below its inversion temperature, and warms above it. For nitrogen the maximum inversion temperature is about 621 K, so it cools on expansion at room temperature, and for hydrogen (about 204 K) and helium (about 40 K) it must first be precooled. This is the basis of the Linde process for liquefying gases.

quiz.q: What is (∂U/∂V)_T for an ideal gas?

entries.name: Equations of state, the virial expansion and critical constants
entries.tagline: How real gases depart from PV = nRT, and where the liquid–gas critical point comes from.

equations: Z = pV_m ÷ RT = 1 + B(T) ÷ V_m + C(T) ÷ V_m² + …
sections.text: For an ideal gas Z = 1 at all conditions. The virial equation expresses deviations as a series in 1/V_m. The second virial coefficient B reflects pair interactions: B is negative at low temperatures, where attraction dominates, and positive at high temperatures, where repulsion dominates. The Boyle temperature is where B = 0, and there the gas is nearly ideal over a range of pressures.

Below T_c the van der Waals isotherm has a loop corresponding to liquid–gas coexistence. At T_c the loop shrinks to a point of inflection. Z_c = p_cV_c/RT_c = 3/8 = 0.375, a little above the typical measured values of about 0.27–0.29.
For CO₂, a = 3.64 L²·bar/mol² and b = 0.0427 L/mol. T_c = 8 × 3.64 ÷ (27 × 0.08314 × 0.0427) ≈ 304 K, close to the measured 304.1 K.

If pressure, volume and temperature are written as fractions of the critical values (reduced variables), many different gases follow approximately the same equation of state. This is the law of corresponding states, and it explains why generalized compressibility charts work.
The fugacity f = φp replaces pressure in the chemical potential of a real gas, so that thermodynamic formulas keep their form. φ is the fugacity coefficient, and it tends to 1 at low pressure.

quiz.q: What is the critical compressibility factor Z_c predicted by the van der Waals equation?

entries.name: Chemical potential and partial molar quantities
entries.tagline: The quantity that decides which way matter flows between phases and in reactions.

equations: dG = −S dT + V dp + Σ μᵢ dnᵢ
sections.text: The chemical potential of component i is its partial molar Gibbs energy: how G changes when a little more of i is added at constant T and p. Matter flows from high μ to low μ, just as heat flows from high T to low T.

points: At phase equilibrium, μᵢ of each component is the same in every phase.
At chemical equilibrium, Σ νᵢ μᵢ = 0 for the reaction.
For an ideal gas, μ = μ° + RT ln(p/p°). For a real gas, p is replaced by the fugacity.
For a solute in solution, μ = μ° + RT ln a, where a is the activity.

sections.text: In a mixture, the volume contributed by each component is not generally its pure molar volume. Mixing 50 mL of ethanol with 50 mL of water gives only about 96 mL, because the partial molar volumes of the two are smaller in the mixture, due to hydrogen bonding.

equations: Σ nᵢ dμᵢ = 0   (constant T and p)
sections.text: The chemical potentials of the components of a mixture cannot all change independently. In a binary mixture, if μ of one component rises, that of the other falls, which lets one be calculated from the other.

quiz.q: At phase equilibrium, what is true of the chemical potential of a component?
quiz.a: It is the same in every phase
wrong: It is highest in the liquid

entries.name: Phase equilibria: the phase rule and the Clapeyron equation
entries.tagline: How many variables you can change freely, and how the boiling or melting point depends on pressure.

sections.text: F is the number of degrees of freedom (intensive variables that can be changed independently), C is the number of components and P the number of phases. For water (C = 1): in a single phase F = 2 (T and p are free), on a coexistence line F = 1, and at the triple point F = 0. With a reaction or a constraint, C is the number of independent components.

This gives the slope of any coexistence line on a phase diagram. For melting of ice, ΔV is negative (ice is less dense), so the slope is negative: about −13.5 MPa/K from ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol and ΔV = −1.6 cm³/mol. That is why pressure lowers the melting point of ice.

For vaporization, with the vapor as an ideal gas and the liquid volume neglected. A plot of ln p against 1/T is a line with slope −ΔH_vap/R. It is used to find the enthalpy of vaporization from vapor pressure measurements.

Water boils at 373.15 K at 101.3 kPa with ΔH_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol. At 363.15 K (90 °C): ln(p₂/p₁) = −(40 700 ÷ 8.314)(1/363.15 − 1/373.15) = −0.361, so p₂ = 0.697 × 101.3 ≈ 70.6 kPa. The measured value is 70.1 kPa.
In a two-phase region of a binary phase diagram, the amounts of the two phases are inversely proportional to the distances from the overall composition to the two phase boundaries on the tie line.

quiz.q: How many degrees of freedom does the system have at the triple point of water?
A plot of ln p against 1/T for a vapor pressure curve has a slope of…

entries.name: Ideal and non-ideal solutions
entries.tagline: How mixing changes the energy and entropy, and what happens when molecules do not mix ideally.

equations: ΔG_mix = nRT Σ xᵢ ln xᵢ
sections.text: In an ideal solution the interactions between unlike molecules are the same as between like ones. Mixing is driven entirely by entropy, so ΔG is always negative and the components are miscible in all proportions. Raoult's law holds for all components.
The activity replaces the mole fraction: μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln aᵢ, where aᵢ = γᵢxᵢ. The activity coefficient γ measures the departure from ideality.
points: Positive deviations (γ > 1): unlike interactions weaker than like ones, so the vapor pressure is higher than expected, and ΔH_mix is positive. At the extreme, the liquids do not mix.
Negative deviations (γ < 1): unlike interactions stronger, so the vapor pressure is lower, and ΔH_mix is negative.
Solute at low concentration follows Henry's law, with a different constant, while the solvent follows Raoult's law.

sections.text: With large deviations, the boiling point curve has a maximum or minimum, where the vapor and the liquid have the same composition. Distillation cannot separate beyond that point. Ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope at 95.6% ethanol (78.2 °C). Hydrochloric acid and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope at about 20% HCl (108.6 °C).

Ions interact strongly over long distances, so even dilute solutions are non-ideal. The Debye–Hückel limiting law gives the mean activity coefficient of an electrolyte: log γ± = −0.509 |z₊z₋| √I at 25 °C in water, where I is the ionic strength, I = ½ Σ cᵢzᵢ². It works up to about 0.01 M.

quiz.q: What drives the mixing of an ideal solution?
quiz.a: Entropy only, since ΔH is zero

entries.name: Chemical equilibrium and the van 't Hoff equation
entries.tagline: Linking ΔG° to K, and K to temperature.

sections.text: At equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K. K is exponentially sensitive to ΔG°, as K = e^(−ΔG°/RT). At 298 K, a ΔG° of −5.7 kJ/mol corresponds to K ≈ 10, and every extra 5.7 kJ/mol multiplies K by another factor of 10.

This is the van 't Hoff equation. A plot of ln K against 1/T is a straight line, with slope −ΔH°/R and intercept ΔS°/R, so measuring K at several temperatures gives ΔH° and ΔS° (assuming they are constant).

points: Endothermic reactions (ΔH° > 0): K increases with temperature.

Exothermic reactions (ΔH° < 0): K decreases with temperature. For ammonia synthesis, Kp falls from about 6 × 10⁵ atm⁻² at 298 K to about 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ atm⁻² at 773 K, which is why the industrial process is a compromise with the rate.
This is Le Chatelier's principle, derived.

quiz.q: A plot of ln K against 1/T has a slope equal to…
What happens to K for an exothermic reaction as temperature rises?

entries.name: Thermodynamics of electrochemical cells
entries.tagline: A cell voltage is a direct measurement of free energy.

sections.text: The Nernst equation is properly written with activities, not concentrations.
ln K = nFE° ÷ RT. For the Zn–Cu cell (E° = 1.10 V, n = 2), log K = 2 × 1.10 ÷ 0.0592 = 37.2, so K ≈ 10³⁷, and the reaction goes essentially to completion.

sections.h: Entropy and enthalpy from the temperature coefficient
sections.text: Measuring how the cell potential changes with temperature gives the entropy of the cell reaction, and with it ΔH.

A cell with the same electrodes in solutions of different concentration has E° = 0, but a voltage E = (RT/nF) ln(c₂/c₁). This is how a pH or ion-selective electrode works, and nerve cells use the same principle with ions across a membrane.

In practice, the measured 'formal potential' (the potential at 1 M under stated conditions of ionic strength and pH) is used, because activity coefficients are hard to separate. Activities are estimated with the Debye–Hückel equation.

quiz.q: How is the entropy change of a cell reaction found from cell measurements?
quiz.a: From the temperature coefficient of the cell potential
wrong: From the cell potential at one temperature

entries.name: The Boltzmann distribution
entries.tagline: How molecules are spread across energy levels at a given temperature.

sections.text: Thermodynamics treats matter in bulk. Statistical mechanics explains it from the properties of molecules. The central result is the Boltzmann distribution, which gives the population of each energy level for a system in thermal equilibrium.

equations: Nᵢ ÷ Nⱼ = (gᵢ ÷ gⱼ) e^(−(εᵢ − εⱼ) ÷ kT)
sections.text: g is the degeneracy of the level, k = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant, and W is the number of microstates (ways of arranging the molecules) consistent with the macroscopic state. The Boltzmann distribution is the arrangement with the greatest W, subject to fixed total number of molecules and total energy.

points: The scale for thermal energy is kT. At 298 K, kT = 4.1 × 10⁻²¹ J, which is 207 cm⁻¹, or RT = 2.48 kJ/mol.
Levels with energy much greater than kT are almost empty, and levels much lower are almost fully occupied. Higher temperature flattens the distribution.
Example: two levels 1000 cm⁻¹ apart at 298 K have population ratio e^(−1000/207) = 0.008, so about 0.8% of molecules are in the upper level.
A system at infinite temperature has all levels equally populated (per state), and at absolute zero all molecules are in the ground state.

sections.text: S = k ln W links the macroscopic entropy to counting. A bigger W means higher entropy, so a gas expanding into a bigger volume or a solid melting increases W. It is inscribed on Boltzmann's gravestone.

quiz.q: In the Boltzmann distribution, what happens to the population of an excited level as temperature rises?

entries.name: The partition function
entries.tagline: One function that contains all the thermodynamics of a system.

sections.text: The molecular partition function q is a sum over all the energy levels of one molecule, each weighted by its Boltzmann factor. It is roughly the number of thermally accessible states.

points: The fraction of molecules in level i is pᵢ = gᵢ e^(−εᵢ/kT) ÷ q.
At T → 0, q → g₀ (only the ground state). At T → ∞, q → the total number of states.
For N independent, distinguishable particles (atoms in a crystal), the system partition function is Q = q^N.
For N indistinguishable particles (a gas), Q = q^N ÷ N!. The N! corrects for the overcounting of identical molecules.
For interacting particles, Q has to be calculated from the full energy levels of the system. The set of all possible copies of the system is the canonical ensemble.

sections.text: Once Q is known, every thermodynamic property follows by differentiation. That is the power of the method: the properties of a macroscopic system from the energy levels of its molecules.

quiz.q: For N indistinguishable particles in a gas, the partition function Q is…

entries.name: Translational, rotational and vibrational partition functions
entries.tagline: Because the motions are independent, q is a product, and each part is simple.

sections.text: The energies of the different degrees of freedom add, so the partition functions multiply. Each is evaluated separately.

Λ is the thermal de Broglie wavelength. Translational levels are so closely spaced that the sum can be replaced by an integral. At room temperature q_trans is enormous, about 10²⁷ for a molecule in a mole-size volume.

equations: q_rot = T ÷ (σ Θ_rot)    (linear molecule, T ≫ Θ_rot)
sections.text: σ is the symmetry number: 1 for a heteronuclear diatomic (HCl) and 2 for a homonuclear one (N₂), counting indistinguishable orientations. For HCl, Θ_rot = 10.6 × 1.4388 = 15.2 K, so at room temperature many rotational levels are populated.

equations: q_vib = 1 ÷ (1 − e^(−Θ_vib/T))    (zero of energy at the lowest level)
sections.text: For HCl, Θ_vib = 2990 × 1.4388 ≈ 4300 K, far above room temperature, so q_vib ≈ 1: nearly all molecules are in the vibrational ground state. Vibration is 'frozen out'.
Usually q_elec = g₀, the degeneracy of the electronic ground state, since excited states are far above kT.

The entropy of a monatomic ideal gas, from translation alone. For argon at 298 K and 1 bar it gives 154.8 J/(mol·K), in excellent agreement with experiment, which was a triumph of statistical mechanics.

quiz.q: Why is the vibrational partition function of HCl about 1 at room temperature?
quiz.a: Θ_vib is much greater than T, so only the ground state is populated
wrong: Vibrational levels are too closely spaced

quiz.q: What is the rotational symmetry number of N₂?

entries.name: Equipartition and heat capacities
entries.tagline: Why gases and solids have the heat capacities they do, and why they change with temperature.

sections.text: The equipartition theorem says that at high enough temperature, each quadratic term in the energy of a molecule contributes ½kT to the average energy (and ½R to the molar heat capacity).

facts: 3 translations + 2 rotations = (5/2)R. Vibration is frozen out, because the spacing is much more than kT.
Vibration adds R (two quadratic terms), giving (7/2)R.
3 translations + 3 rotations = 3R, plus vibrations when they are excited.

sections.text: The Dulong–Petit law says that atoms in a crystal, which have three vibrational degrees of freedom each, give a molar heat capacity of 3R = 24.9 J/(mol·K). It holds for many metals at room temperature. At low temperatures the heat capacity falls toward zero, which classical physics could not explain.

points: Einstein model: all atoms vibrate at one frequency. C_V = 3R (Θ_E/T)² e^(Θ_E/T) ÷ (e^(Θ_E/T) − 1)². It reproduces the fall at low T, though too steeply.
Debye model: a range of frequencies, as in real crystals. It gives C_V ∝ T³ at low temperatures, which agrees with experiment (the Debye T³ law).
Substances with a high Debye temperature have low heat capacity at room temperature. Diamond, with Θ_D about 2200 K, has C_V of only about 6 J/(mol·K) at 298 K.

quiz.q: What is C_V of a diatomic gas at room temperature, treating vibration as frozen?
What does the Dulong–Petit law predict for the molar heat capacity of a solid?

entries.name: Statistical entropy, residual entropy and equilibrium constants
entries.tagline: Counting states explains entropy values, the third law, and K.

sections.text: For a reaction in the gas phase, K can be calculated from the partition functions of the reactants and products and the difference in their ground-state energies:
points: q° is the molar partition function per unit volume, evaluated at standard pressure.
ΔE₀ is the difference in energy between the lowest levels of products and reactants.

It explains the temperature dependence of K and isotope exchange equilibria, such as H₂ + D₂ ⇌ 2HD, where K is near 4 at high temperature because HD has twice as many accessible rotational states as H₂ or D₂ (symmetry numbers).

sections.text: The third law says S = 0 at 0 K for a perfect crystal. If a crystal is frozen with a degree of disorder, it keeps a residual entropy of k ln W.
points: Carbon monoxide: molecules can point CO or OC in the lattice. If each is random, W = 2^N and S = R ln 2 = 5.8 J/(mol·K). The measured value is about 4.6.

Ice: each oxygen has four hydrogen-bonded neighbors but the hydrogens can be placed in several ways satisfying the 'ice rules'. Pauling estimated S = R ln(3/2) = 3.4 J/(mol·K), in agreement with the measured 3.4.

sections.text: ΔS_mix = −nR Σ xᵢ ln xᵢ is the statistical result of the number of ways of arranging two kinds of molecules on a lattice. For an equimolar mixture it is R ln 2 per mole of molecules, or 5.76 J/(mol·K).

quiz.q: What is the residual entropy of a crystal with two equally likely orientations per molecule?
